codes.total_rationale: No total score is reported; the two dimensions were modelled separately. Any combined score would cover two types: instrumental/task reliance (T2) and emotional reliance (T3). No item text was available to check whether one type is the majority, so the total is T4 (mixed).

subscales.name: Instrumental Dependence (ID)
subscales.rationale: Typed from the subscale name only. 'Instrumental dependence' on conversational AI means relying on it to get tasks done, which is functional dependence. No item text was available to confirm this; probably 6–7 items (ID2–ID7 in Table 2).

subscales.name: Emotional Dependence (ED)
subscales.rationale: Typed from the subscale name only. 'Emotional dependence' on conversational AI matches emotional reliance and attachment. No item text was available to confirm this; 7 items (ED1–ED7).

codes.note: R0506 prints no item text and the development paper wasn't available, so nothing could be quoted. Vietnamese translation adapted to work use. ID1 may have been dropped. The types depend on the names only; check them against the items in Li et al. (2026).

codes.total_rationale: The total is the sum of two equal 6-item subscales of different types. Instrumental Dependency is mostly functional reliance on the LLM for decisions (T2). Relationship Dependency is about companionship and emotional bonding (T3). Neither type has a clear majority across the 12 items (about 4 T2, 6 T3, 2 addiction-like), so the total is mixed.

subscales.name: Instrumental Dependency (ID1–ID6)
subscales.rationale: Four of six items are about relying on the LLM for decisions and unease or low confidence without it (ID1, ID4, ID5, ID6). Two items are addiction-like: ID2 (losing track of time, loss of control) and ID3 (feeling rewarded, mood modification). T2 is the majority type.

subscales.name: Relationship Dependency (RD1–RD6)
subscales.rationale: All items are about self-disclosure, treating the LLM as a companion, feeling less alone, and its social role. RD5 is reverse-scored and asks about expressing feelings. These are emotional or companionship dependence.

quoted_items: ID5: It is my go-to for assistance in decision-making
ID6: Making decisions without it feels somewhat uneasy
RD2: I interact with it as if it were a genuine companion
RD3: It helps me feel less alone when I need to talk to someone
codes.note: ID2 (time immersion, loss of control) and ID3 (reward, mood modification) are T1-like minority items within the Instrumental subscale. A separate T2 or T3 subscale analysis is recommended rather than using the total score.

codes.total_rationale: The 11-item total is built on Goodman's behavioural-addiction model. 8 of its 11 items fall in addiction-component subscales: withdrawal (4) and negative consequences (4). The printed withdrawal items describe irritability and disconnection when the AI can't be accessed. The 3 cognitive-preoccupation items, judged from their one printed item, read as functional reliance in decision-making. So the majority type is T1, with a minority of T2-like content.

subscales.name: Cognitive preoccupation (3 items; one report calls it 'cognitive distress')
subscales.rationale: The name is an addiction component (salience), but the only printed item ('My decisions are mostly/often influenced by generative AI') is about handing decisions over to AI, which is functional dependence. This rests on one item, so it is uncertain; if typed by name alone it would be T1.

subscales.name: Negative consequences (4 items)
subscales.rationale: Named after an addiction component (conflict/negative consequences). No item text is printed, so the evidence is the subscale name only.

subscales.name: Withdrawal (4 items)
subscales.rationale: The items describe withdrawal-like irritability and disconnection when the AI can't be used, e.g., 'I get frustrated or irritable when I am unable to use generative AI'. Typed from item content.

quoted_items: I get frustrated or irritable when I am unable to use generative AI
I feel a sense of disconnection when I cannot access generative artificial intelligence.
My decisions are mostly influenced by generative artificial intelligence
codes.note: Only 4 item texts are printed and the development paper wasn't available. One report treats the scale as single-factor. Another describes it as covering 'emotional attachment' and 'AI opinion/study/creativity', which may be a different version; check. The 9-item version may differ.

codes.total_rationale: The 5 DAI items don't share one type. Item 2 (falling behind on tasks without AI) and item 4 (needing AI feedback to feel confident in decisions) are about functional or cognitive reliance (T2). Item 1 (feeling unprotected without access to AI) is like withdrawal or emotional distress. Item 3 (keeping up with AI to stay relevant) and item 5 (fear that AI will replace one's skills) are about FOMO or AI anxiety and fit none of the types. No type has a clear majority, so the total is T4.
quoted_items: I feel unprotected when I do not have access to AI.
I'm concerned about the idea of being left behind in my tasks or projects if I do not use AI.
I constantly need validation or feedback from AI systems to feel confident in my decisions.
I fear that AI might replace my current skills or abilities.
codes.note: Single factor; no subscales. Versions differ: R-AID1 is positively worded ('feel protected'), and the AIGD version has 4 items. The 'Addiction' name and DSM-5 claims don't change the type. The 'multidimensional' Perceived AI Dependency scale may be another instrument.

codes.total_rationale: Single total score. Most printed items are Bergen/Griffiths addiction components: salience (thinking about CAI a lot), tolerance or excessive use (using it more than one should), loss of control or relapse (failing to cut down), and withdrawal (uneasy when unable to use it). One item, about reliance interfering with doing tasks without AI, is T2-like. As it is a single item, the majority type T1 holds.
quoted_items: I tried to reduce my use of CAI but was unsuccessful.
I spend a lot of time thinking about CAI
I feel uneasy or frustrated when I am unable to use generative AI tools.
codes.note: One report labels this 'emotional addiction', but the items are addiction-type, not about emotional support (T3). The teacher GenAI version (PGAIU) has one T2-like reliance item. Item counts differ between reports (4–6). No subscales were reported.

codes.total_rationale: The included report doesn't print any item text for C1–C6, and the scale is a single total with no subscales, so there's no item content to type from. The protocol types by item content, not by the scale's name or source. That makes this T4 (unclear) by default. Because the items were adapted from the SAS and CIAS, which are addiction scales, it's probably T1. But that can't be confirmed without the items.
codes.note: No items are available and there's no development paper. The source scales (Kwon 2013 SAS, Chen 2003 CIAS) suggest addiction-type content, likely T1. The R4868 authors should be asked for C1–C6 so the type can be re-checked.

codes.total_rationale: The scale is a single 'addiction' construct adapted from a fast-food addiction measure (Farah & Shahzad, 2020). The only printed item describes worry or preoccupation about not using the app, which is the salience/withdrawal component of behavioural addiction. The item mentions an 'AI friend', but it asks about distress at not using the app, not about relying on it for emotional support. So this is addiction-type.
quoted_items: Not chatting to my AI friend is something I worry about
codes.note: Weak evidence: only 1 of the 7 retained items is printed, and the development paper isn't available. The T1 call rests on that one item plus the addiction source. No subscales were reported.

codes.total_rationale: No item texts are printed and there is no development paper. The only evidence is the factor names. They point in different directions: Practical/Applied suggests functional reliance, Cognitive/Affective mixes cognitive and emotional reliance, and Direct Interaction is unclear. No single type can be shown to make up most of the items, so the total score is T4.

subscales.name: Direct Interaction Reliance (DIR; Q2, Q3, Q4, Q5, Q12)
subscales.rationale: The name does not match any addiction component, task-reliance construct or emotional construct. 'Reliance' on interacting with AI could be functional, emotional or habitual. No item text is available.

subscales.name: Practical/Applied Dependency (PAD; Q6–Q10)
subscales.rationale: Tentative, based on the name only. 'Practical/applied' dependency suggests relying on AI to carry out tasks, which is functional dependence. Reclassify if the item texts become available.

subscales.name: Cognitive/Affective Reliance (CAR; Q1, Q11, Q13–Q15)
subscales.rationale: The name combines cognitive reliance (T2) and affective reliance (T3) in one factor. Without item texts there is no way to tell which type has the majority.

codes.note: The included report gives no item texts, so nothing is quoted. Types are based only on the EFA factor names. PAD = T2 is low-confidence. Get the Ai-Dep items from the R0691 authors or supplement to confirm the types.

codes.total_rationale: None of the included reports print any of the 18 items, and no subscales are reported, so there is no item content to type from. The labels 'AI reliance' and 'reliance on AI dialogue' hint at functional dependence (T2), but the protocol types by item content, not by the scale's name. Under the rule for having no item text and no subscale content, the total score is T4.
codes.note: The authors wrote this 18-item scale themselves (Prasad et al., 2026). Scored 18-90 with low/moderate/high cut-offs (Table 2, p. 5). No development paper; not adapted from another scale. Get the items from the authors or the supplement to reclassify; the label suggests T2.

codes.total_rationale: None of the included reports print any item texts, and there is no development paper. The only content information is the names of the three EFA factors. Taken together, those names point to reliance on AI for tasks (T2) and possibly to affective or emotional reliance (T3). No single type can be shown to hold a majority, so the total Ai-Dep score is typed T4: mixed or unclear.

subscales.name: Direct Interaction Reliance (DIR; Q2-Q5, Q12)
subscales.rationale: The name does not refer to any addiction component, and it does not make clear whether the reliance is functional or emotional. With no item text available, the subscale cannot be typed, so it is T4.

subscales.name: Practical/Applied Dependency (PAD; Q6-Q10)
subscales.rationale: Provisional, based only on the name. 'Practical/applied dependency' suggests relying on AI to carry out tasks, which is functional dependence. The item content still needs to be checked.

subscales.name: Cognitive/Affective Reliance (CAR; Q1, Q11, Q13-Q15)
subscales.rationale: The name covers two types at once: cognitive reliance (T2) and affective reliance (T3). Without item texts, the balance between them cannot be judged, so it is T4.

codes.note: No items were available to quote. This appears to be an ad hoc scale written by the authors (Elsayed, Al-Mutairi & Moussa, 2026). The typing should be redone once the item texts for Q1-Q15 have been obtained, either from the published article's supplement or from the authors.

codes.total_rationale: Item content does not point to one type. The 6-item development version is based on the Bergen Facebook Addiction Scale (Andreassen 2012), and its sample item is about failing to cut down (T1). The 5-item versions in the included reports mix withdrawal-like anxiety about tasks (T1/T2) with difficulty doing work without AI (T2). One report also lists emotional dependence and a need for AI validation (T3). No type clearly dominates.
quoted_items: I tried to reduce the use of ChatGPT without success
I feel anxious when I cannot use AI tools to complete academic tasks
Without AI support, I find it difficult to accomplish academic tasks.
I feel anxious when I am unable to use GenAI to complete learning tasks.
codes.note: The 5-item versions in the reports differ from the 6-item Bergen-based original, and only 3 of their items are printed. If a full item list shows the 5-item version is mostly task-focused, retype it as T2. If the Bergen-based 6-item original is used, type it T1.

codes.total_rationale: No item texts are available. Both subscales are about how capable and confident students feel in academic work without AI, i.e. difficulty working or studying without AI (functional dependence). The 'phobia' in the scale name suggests something like withdrawal, but the protocol types by content, not by name. Neither subscale is named after an addiction component or an emotional bond, so the total gets their common type, T2. Based on subscale names only.

subscales.name: Academic Self-Efficacy Anxiety
subscales.rationale: The name points to anxiety about one's own ability to do academic work, presumably without AI. That is task-performance dependence, not an addiction component or an emotional bond. Evidence: subscale name only.

subscales.name: Lack of Academic Confidence without AI
subscales.rationale: The name explicitly refers to low confidence in doing academic work without AI, which matches T2 (difficulty working or thinking without AI). Evidence: subscale name only.

codes.note: The included report gives no item texts, and the development paper (Gezgin & Türk Kurtça, 2025) was not available. Typing is provisional: if the 18 items include fear or withdrawal-style anxiety items, the total could become T4 or partly T1. Check the items against the development paper.

codes.total_rationale: All 13 items follow ICD-11 addictive-behaviour criteria: impaired control (using longer than planned, failing to cut down), increasing priority (replacing activities, putting off meals or sleep), continuing despite negative consequences, and impairment. The two distress items ('to feel better', 'first things you do when distressed') are mood modification, also an addiction component. No item asks about relying on AI for tasks or about an attachment bond.

subscales.name: Impaired control
subscales.rationale: Loss of control and relapse: 'Do you often end up using the chatbot longer than you planned?' and 'Have you tried to reduce or stop, but couldn't?'

subscales.name: Increasing priority
subscales.rationale: Salience: use replaces hobbies, friends and homework, and meals or sleep get postponed. Also includes mood-modification items (using it first when distressed).

subscales.name: Continuation despite negative consequences
subscales.rationale: Conflict and negative consequences: sleep problems, worse concentration or school performance, conflict at home, and 'Do you keep using it even when you notice these problems?'

subscales.name: Clinically significant impairment/therapeutic interference
subscales.rationale: The ICD-11 impairment criterion, covering harm to daily life or treatment, whether problems would improve without use, and ruling out other causes. This is the negative-consequences component of addiction.

quoted_items: Do you often end up using the chatbot longer than you planned?
Have you tried to reduce or stop, but couldn't?
Has chatbot use replaced activities you used to do, such as hobbies, friends, sports, or homework?
Do you keep using it even when you notice these problems?
codes.note: Clinician interview built for R0953 from ICD-11 gaming disorder guidance. The report gave no item-to-domain mapping, so items were assigned to domains by content. The distress items fit mood modification (T1), not emotional dependence (T3).

codes.total_rationale: Most printed items in this family follow Bergen/Griffiths components: salience (PACU1), tolerance (PACU2), relapse/failed cut-down (PACU3, PED1), withdrawal (PACU4, PED2), conflict/negative consequences (PACU5) and loss of control (PED3). The family is T1 by majority. Two variants depart from this: PED4–PED6 are emotional-attachment items (T3), and some AID inventory items are about functional reliance (T2).
quoted_items: PACU3. I tried to cut down on the use of AI chatbots but failed.
PACU4. I become restless or troubled if I have been prohibited from using AI chatbots.
I feel annoyed, upset, or depressed when I can't use an AI chatbot.
PED5. I have developed a special emotional attachment to my AI companion and increasingly need it to maintain my emotional stability.
codes.note: No subscales scored. Variants differ: the PED scale is split 3 T1 (PED1–3) and 3 T3 (PED4–6), so T4 at report level. The 24-item AID inventory adds T2 items (grammar, writing) and needs a check per report. The other variants are T1.

codes.total_rationale: The report prints only one of the 7 items (DE1–DE7). That item is about finding tasks harder to complete without AI, which is functional dependence and fits T2. Both source scales were built for university students' academic use of AI. The one item does not show a majority, so this typing is provisional. If the remaining items include withdrawal-type or emotional content, the total could be T1 or T4.
quoted_items: I feel that completing tasks becomes more difficult when I do not use AI.
codes.note: Low confidence: only 1 of 7 items is available. Check DE2–DE7 against Morales-García et al. (2024) and Wu et al. (2026). Downgrade to T4 if the items cover more than one type. No subscales; single total score (α = .954).

codes.total_rationale: The included report prints none of the 4 items, there is no development paper, and the scale has no subscales. The only clue is the authors' description: 'behavioral over-reliance and cognitive offloading'. That suggests functional dependence (T2), but the protocol decides type by item content, so a construct description isn't enough. With no items and no subscale content, the score is T4 (unclear).
codes.note: Likely T2 from the stated construct (over-reliance, cognitive offloading), but no item text was available. Re-type if R1120's appendix or the authors supply the items. Single factor: α=0.91, AVE=0.71.

codes.total_rationale: None of the 8 item texts are printed in R1130, and no subscales are reported, so the item content can't be checked. Under the protocol the scale name 'Perceived AI Dependency' can't decide the type, and it could fit functional (T2), emotional (T3) or addiction-type (T1) content. It is therefore T4 (unclear).
codes.note: Adapted from Zhang et al. (ref. 41), but the reference list isn't in the retrieved text. Recommend retrieving R1130's full reference list or supplement to identify the source scale and its items, then re-type.

codes.total_rationale: This is a provisional T2. No item texts were printed. The only basis is the report's summary of what the 10-item total score covers: relying on AI for academic tasks, putting in less independent effort, and difficulty working without AI. All three match the T2 definition of relying on AI for study tasks or thinking and finding it hard to work without it. The summary mentions no addiction components and no emotional or companionship content.
codes.note: T2 rests on the authors' summary of the scale's content, not on item text, and there are no items to quote. Under a strict items-only rule this would be T4. Check the T2 against the R0247 questionnaire or appendix if you can get it. The scale is single-score (range 10-50) with no subscales.

codes.total_rationale: No item texts are printed and no subscales are reported for the chatbot adaptation. Under the protocol, a name like 'problematic use' cannot set the type, so this is T4 for lack of evidence. Likely T1 if items are found: the source GPIUS2 (Caplan 2010) covers preoccupation, compulsive use, mood regulation, negative outcomes and preference for online social interaction. The discussion also mentions loss of control and negative mood when access is unavailable.
codes.note: Source structure is from general knowledge of GPIUS2, not from R3792. Unknown if the scale was shortened or items dropped. Get the adapted items from R3792's authors or supplement; if they follow GPIUS2, retype the total as T1 (POSI items are the minority).

codes.total_rationale: Only 2 of the 10 items are printed. One is a clear withdrawal item ("anxious if I can't use"). The other reads as overuse or a negative consequence (using AI where a human professional is needed), though it could also be read as functional over-reliance. The scale is adapted from the Smartphone Addiction Scale, whose items all cover addiction components such as daily-life disturbance, withdrawal, overuse and tolerance. That supports T1, but with limited certainty.
quoted_items: I feel anxious if I can't use my mental health AI app
I use the AI for things that obviously require a human professional
codes.note: Only 2 of 10 items available; no development paper. The withdrawal item decides T1. Item 2 is ambiguous between T1 (overuse) and T2 (over-reliance). No attachment items shown, so not T3. If more items surface, T4 is possible.

codes.total_rationale: Unidimensional 5-item scale. The reported item topics are over-reliance on AI, copying without understanding, dependency, shortcut usage and lack of critical evaluation. All are about relying on or handing off tasks and thinking to AI (functional dependence). None suggest addiction components (salience, withdrawal, loss of control) or emotional or companionship reliance. Typed from item-topic descriptions, not verbatim items.
codes.note: No item texts available. Only topic descriptions for the 5 items, so no quotes given. 'Dependency' item is ambiguous; T2 holds by majority. Verify wording in OSF Extended Data (doi 10.17605/OSF.IO/TFMGQ). 'subscale_names' is the closest fit, as there are no subscales.

codes.total_rationale: No item wording is printed, but the report describes the 4 indicators. Three are addiction components: perceived overuse, difficulty limiting use (loss of control) and unease or frustration when GA is unavailable (withdrawal). The fourth, interference with independent task completion, is functional dependence (T2) or possibly a negative consequence (T1). With 3 or more of 4 indicators addiction-type, T1 is the majority. The construct is adapted from 'Generative AI Addiction'.
codes.note: No item texts; typed from the reported descriptions of the 4 indicators in a single-factor scale. No items quoted, to avoid inventing any. One indicator (interference with independent tasks) may be T2. Check against the full item wording if found (Du et al., 2026).

codes.total_rationale: This family groups different instruments whose content differs. The 4 printed items come from the ADS-R and the 7-item coursework ADS. They are functional (T2): not being able to work or think without AI, and AI as an external brain. AIAT-20 and CIAT-10 are close rewordings of Young's IAT, which is addiction-type (T1). CIAT-10's content map lists withdrawal and preoccupation, but no AIAT/CIAT item text is printed. No single type holds across the family, so T4.

subscales.name: Y_FunctionalDep: Cognitive Integration and Habit (ADS-R, 9 items)
subscales.rationale: The name and the printed ADS-R items describe AI built into one's thinking and work as an external brain. That is cognitive reliance. 'Habit' does not name an addiction component.

subscales.name: Y_AutonomyLoss: Autonomy Erosion and Life Proxy (ADS-R, 6 items)
subscales.rationale: The name describes handing judgement and life tasks over to AI. The printed item 'can't work/think without AI' fits difficulty functioning without AI. Item-to-subscale assignment is not reported.

quoted_items: I feel AI has become an indispensable part of my knowledge system or external brain
People around me have commented that I can't work/think without AI
I often find myself relying on AI tools more than intended when completing coursework.
codes.note: Type each version separately. ADS-R 15 items and ADS 7 items: T2, from items. AIAT-20/CIAT-10: probably T1 (IAT-derived; CIAT-10 map lists withdrawal, preoccupation), no item text. 'More than intended' item mixes T1 wording with T2 content.

codes.total_rationale: No item texts are available. The stated content domains of the 8-item pool cross types. Loss of control, failed reduction, compulsive checking and excessive time use are T1, which is about half the pool and not a clear majority. Overreliance and reduced independent thinking are T2, academic avoidance is ambiguous (T2 or T1), and emotional dependence is T3. With no clear majority type, the total is T4.

subscales.name: Loss of control (LPA core subdimension)
subscales.rationale: The name matches the addiction component relapse/loss of control. Evidence is the subscale name only; item count not reported.

subscales.name: Compulsive use (LPA core subdimension)
subscales.rationale: The name matches the addiction component compulsive use. Evidence is the subscale name only; item count not reported.

subscales.name: Academic avoidance (LPA core subdimension)
subscales.rationale: Only the name is known. It could mean handing academic work to AI (T2) or harm to studies (T1 conflict/negative consequences). The type can't be decided without item text.

codes.note: Item texts were not printed and the development paper is unavailable, so no items are quoted. If item texts turn up and show 5 or more T1 items, retype the total as T1. The LPA subdimensions are not formally scored subscales.

codes.total_rationale: The report prints none of the 18 items. The only content information is the names of the two dimensions: functional dependence and existential dependence. Functional dependence suggests T2. Existential dependence is not clearly any single type, and the number of items per dimension is not reported. With no items to read and two dimensions that may be different types, the total score cannot be given a majority type, so it is T4.

subscales.name: Functional dependence
subscales.rationale: Typed from the name only. 'Functional dependence' matches the T2 construct of relying on AI to do tasks. No items were seen to confirm this, and the item count is not reported.

subscales.name: Existential dependence
subscales.rationale: Typed from the name only. The name matches no single type. It could mean emotional or attachment-like reliance (T3), or reliance for meaning or identity, which none of the types covers. There are no items or definition to decide between these.

codes.note: Li et al. (37) was not found in the retrieved text. If its items show the 'existential' items are emotional or companionship items, that subscale becomes T3. The total stays T4 unless one dimension clearly has most items.

codes.total_rationale: Both printed items are written as behavioural-addiction components. A failed attempt to cut down is loss of control/relapse, and relying on ChatGPT "more and more" is tolerance (escalating use). The context is academic tasks, which looks functional, but the items measure addiction components rather than difficulty working without AI. This rests on only 2 of the 6 items, so it is tentative.
quoted_items: I tried to reduce my use of ChatGPT to help with my assignment, but I failed
I feel that I relied on using ChatGPT to help complete my academic task more and more.
codes.note: Only 2 of 6 items are printed. The base scale is unnamed and the references are empty. Unidimensional (ω=0.863), no subscales. If the other 4 items turn out to be about reliance on AI for tasks (T2), re-type as T4 or T2.

codes.total_rationale: The included report prints no item texts, names no subscales and cites no development paper. The scale name, 'dependence to AI tools', cannot set the type because the protocol types by item content. With no content to judge from, the total score is T4 (unclear).
codes.note: A researcher-made scale with 12 items scored 1-4 (total range 12-48) and a single total score. No item text appears in R3196. If the authors can supply the items, re-type it; the word 'tools' in the name may point to T2, but that is not evidence.

codes.total_rationale: I had only the subscale names to go on. The 11-item total (ЗІЗ) combines three factors, and each one points to a different type: intimacy and anthropomorphisation, 4 items (T3); cognitive atrophy and loss of autonomy, 3 items (T2); loss of control and maladaptive coping, 3 items (T1). Item 6 is a reverse-scored control item on critical thinking. The split is 4/3/3, so no type has a clear majority, which makes the total mixed (T4).

subscales.name: Factor А: Штучна інтимність та антропоморфізація (Artificial intimacy and anthropomorphisation; items 1, 2, 7, 9)
subscales.rationale: Based on the subscale name only: intimacy with the AI and treating it as human-like point to an attachment-like or companionship bond.

subscales.name: Factor Б: Когнітивна атрофія та втрата автономності (Cognitive atrophy and loss of autonomy; items 4, 5, 8)
subscales.rationale: Based on the subscale name only: cognitive atrophy and loss of autonomy point to handing thinking over to the AI and relying on it too much.

subscales.name: Factor В: Втрата контролю та дезадаптивний копінг (Loss of control and maladaptive coping; items 3, 10, 11)
subscales.rationale: Based on the subscale name only: loss of control is a behavioural-addiction component, and maladaptive coping is close to mood modification.

codes.note: No item texts are in R2984 and the development paper isn't available, so there is nothing to quote; the types are based on subscale names only. Item 6 (reverse-scored, critical thinking) is a control item outside the factors. Check against the items if the 2026 paper becomes available.

codes.total_rationale: The report prints no item texts and lists no subscales; the items appear only in Supplementary Table S1, which isn't available. The construct definition cites Bozoglan et al. 2014 (problematic Internet use, which points toward T1) and Zhang et al. 2024 (AI dependence in academic contexts, which may point toward T2). The protocol decides type by item content, and with no item content to read, T4 (unclear) is the type assigned.
codes.note: Single unidimensional ad hoc scale (CR = 0.809, AVE = 0.520). Retrieving Supplementary Table S1 of R2637 could settle the type as T1 or T2. Do not infer a type from the cited sources alone.

codes.total_rationale: This is a single, researcher-made Likert item labelled 'GPT Dependence', and its wording is not printed in the included report. The protocol types by item content, not by name. The label alone could fit addiction-type, functional or emotional dependence. With no item text and no subscales to judge from, it is coded T4 (unclear).
codes.note: One of ten 5-point items in an ad hoc ChatGPT perceptions survey (Uppal & Hajian, 2025), scored as one variable (M = 2.861, SD = 1.167). No development paper and no external source. Retype if the item wording can be found, e.g. in supplementary material or from the authors.

codes.total_rationale: Single 5-item total adapted from Smartphone Addiction Scales. Its stated content is subjective dependence, excessive use, harm to studies/relationships (conflict), withdrawal and loss of control/relapse. These are behavioural-addiction components. The two printed items cover loss of control and withdrawal. No item describes task delegation or an emotional bond. T1.
quoted_items: I have tried to reduce the amount of time I spend on AI but failed
I feel anxious and upset when I cannot use artificial intelligence
codes.note: Only 2 of 5 item texts are printed. The other 3 are judged from the authors' description of content (dependence, excessive use, harm to studies/relationships). No subscales. Source refs 80,81 are not in the retrieved text.

codes.total_rationale: No item texts are available. Three of four subscale names match addiction components: Salience, Mood Modification, and Functional Impairment (conflict or negative consequences). The scale is also framed within Griffiths' (2005) model. Excessive Dependency may hold over-reliance (T2) content, but at most it is a minority. This gives a T1 majority from subscale names only. Item counts per subscale are not reported, so confidence is limited.

subscales.name: Salience
subscales.rationale: This is named after Griffiths' salience component. The type rests only on the subscale name.

subscales.name: Mood Modification
subscales.rationale: This is named after Griffiths' mood-modification component. The type rests only on the subscale name.

subscales.name: Excessive Dependency
subscales.rationale: This is not a Griffiths component. Without item text, it could be compulsive or addictive use (T1) or over-reliance on AI for tasks (T2). The name alone cannot settle it.

subscales.name: Functional Impairment
subscales.rationale: The name maps onto the conflict or negative-consequences component in an addiction-framed scale. The type rests only on the subscale name.

codes.note: No items are printed, and the development paper is blinded and not available. These types are provisional. If the development paper is obtained, check the item content of Excessive Dependency (possibly T2) and the number of items in each subscale.

codes.total_rationale: All three reports use only the 5-item Craving subscale of the ADS-9, adapted to refer to AI. Each item is about needing a relationship partner emotionally and being distressed by separation or loss: emptiness when the partner is away, not being able to bear a breakup, always needing them by one's side, and feeling emotionally dependent. That is attachment-like emotional dependence, so the score is T3. The items do not ask about task or thinking reliance, tolerance, conflict or loss of control.
quoted_items: When my partner distances themselves from me (for work, travel, etc.) I feel an unbearable emptiness
I honestly believe that if I broke up with my partner, I would not be able to bear it
I think I am emotionally dependent on my partner
codes.note: Quoted items are the original partner wording (Sirvent-Ruiz 2022, Table 2); no report printed the AI wording. 'Craving' is the source authors' term, but the items describe relational attachment, so content gives T3, not T1. R0724 also drew on Nomura & Kanda's robot-rapport scale; check those items.

codes.total_rationale: The report prints no item texts and names no subscales. It gives only a single 10-item total score (mean, alpha = .90) and no specific source scale. The protocol types by item content, so there is nothing to judge from, which makes this T4 (unclear).
codes.note: Described only as adapted from unnamed earlier studies on AI use and academic procrastination. The academic setting hints at T2 (functional), but this is not item evidence. Retype if R0868's appendix or its authors give the items.

codes.total_rationale: The only printed item describes loss of control, specifically trouble stopping use despite competing priorities, which is a behavioural-addiction component. The report says the 7 items focus on loss of control and preoccupation. The scale is adapted from the PIUQ, an addiction-type measure. Nothing in the report points to functional (task or thinking) reliance or to emotional reliance. Caveat: we read only 1 of the 7 items, so this typing rests partly on the report's description of the content.
quoted_items: I find it difficult to stop using Generative AI even when I know I should focus on other things.
codes.note: Only 1 of 7 items is printed in R1298, and no other item texts are available. The report gives a single total score with no subscales. The development paper is not available.

codes.total_rationale: No item texts are available. Going by subscale names alone, the total combines functional and cognitive dependence (10 items, T2) with emotional dependence (5 items, T3). Five of 15 items is more than the 'one or two' the majority rule allows, so the total spans two types and is coded T4. One source, Yu et al.'s PCGUS, is built on an addiction model, so some items may also be T1 content.

subscales.name: Dependencia Funcional (Functional Dependence)
subscales.rationale: Typed from the name only. 'Functional dependence' matches the T2 definition: relying on AI to carry out tasks. No item texts were available to check this.

subscales.name: Dependencia Emocional (Emotional Dependence)
subscales.rationale: Typed from the name only. 'Emotional dependence' matches T3: relying on AI for emotional support or attachment. No items were available, and the PCGUS source could mean some items are actually mood-modification (T1) content.

subscales.name: Dependencia Cognitiva (Cognitive Dependence)
subscales.rationale: Typed from the name only. 'Cognitive dependence' suggests handing thinking or problem solving over to AI, which is T2. No item texts were available to check this.

codes.note: No items are printed in R0345 and the development paper is unavailable. All types are inferred from subscale names. The item wording should be checked against Morales-García 2024 and Yu 2025 (PCGUS, an addiction-model scale) to confirm there is no T1 content.

codes.total_rationale: All 7 items are about relying on AI to do academic and statistics work: being unable to finish or start tasks without AI, needing AI to check work, and accepting AI output without critical checking. None cover addiction components such as salience, mood modification, tolerance or conflict, and none are emotional or relational. All 7 items are functional dependence.

subscales.name: Difficulty completing academic tasks without AI (4 items)
subscales.rationale: The items describe not being able to finish, start or carry out statistics and assignment work without AI, which is functional dependence. Not knowing how to start when AI is unavailable is a practical problem with the task, not addiction-type withdrawal.

subscales.name: Uncritical acceptance of AI output (3 items)
subscales.rationale: The items describe rarely questioning AI answers and using AI output without checking it. That is over-reliance and handing judgement to AI, which is functional dependence.

quoted_items: I find it hard to finish my assignments without AI tools
Completing a statistical analysis task entirely on my own feels almost impossible
If an AI tool's output looks reasonable, I see no need to verify it against other sources.
codes.note: Written for this study and given in Chinese; the quoted items are the English versions in the report. Only the total score has a reported alpha (0.90); the two domains are content domains. The item about needing AI before feeling confident is about checking work, so it is functional, not emotional.

codes.total_rationale: I could read only one item of the 10 declared. It asks about relying on the AI assistant to cope with difficult emotions, which is emotional dependence (T3). The protocol uses T4 only when there is no item text or subscale content, so T3 is assigned provisionally. A majority could not be checked because the other 9 items are not printed. No addiction-type or task-reliance content is visible, but it cannot be ruled out.
quoted_items: I feel I need my AI assistant to cope with difficult emotions.
codes.note: Low confidence: only 1 of 10 items is printed, and no source or development paper is cited. The scale name was not used for typing. Get the full item list from the R1912 authors to confirm; the type changes to T4 if the remaining items span more than one type.

codes.total_rationale: The included report (R0417) prints no item texts, no subscales are reported (total score only), and the development paper (Hoffmann, Lasarov & Dwivedi, 2024) was not available. Under the protocol, type is decided by item content, not by the scale's name. With no item text and no subscale content, the total score is T4 (unclear).
codes.note: 5-item single scale, translated and adapted into Indonesian. To re-type it, get the item wording from Hoffmann et al. (2024), TFSC 205:123488, or from the R0417 authors. No items were inferred or invented.

codes.total_rationale: At least 8 of the 10 items are about relying on AI to do academic tasks and thinking: starting writing, generating ideas, solving problems, skipping critical thinking, accepting AI answers without checking, and struggling without AI. Item 1 (anxious without AI) sounds like withdrawal but is tied to assignments. Item 9 (stranded if offline) is also about getting the work done. Neither item is about emotional support or compulsive use, so the type is T2.
quoted_items: I rely on AI to start almost every academic writing task.
I find it difficult to generate ideas without the help of AI.
I prefer using AI to solve problems rather than trying to solve them myself first.
I feel anxious when I cannot access AI tools for my assignments.
codes.note: Single 10-item scale with no subscales. There is no development paper, and the source of the items is not given. Items 1 and 9 lean slightly toward withdrawal, but both are about doing academic tasks, so the majority type T2 still holds.

codes.total_rationale: The report prints no item texts and names no subscales, and it cites no development or source paper. Without any content to judge, the protocol classes the single mean score as T4 (unclear). The name 'Dependencia de IA percibida' (perceived AI dependency) can't decide the type, because typing goes by item content, not by the scale's name.
codes.note: Ad hoc Likert scale from R2603 only, scored as one mean (pre M = 2.10, post M = 2.85). No items, subscales or source were reported. Ask the authors for the item texts if it needs to be retyped.

codes.total_rationale: R0490 prints none of the 15 item texts and reports no subscales; it uses a mean score only. The development paper (Kasturiratna & Hartanto, 2026) is not available. The protocol types by item content, not by scale name. With nothing to read, the total score is T4 (unclear).
codes.note: The name ('AI Attachment', used for AI social compensation) points to T3 emotional dependence but cannot decide the type. Get the items from Kasturiratna & Hartanto (2026, CHB Reports 21, 100912) to retype, likely as T3 if confirmed.

codes.total_rationale: The report prints none of the 11 items and lists no subscales, so there is no item content to type from. The label 'AI Overreliance' points to functional dependence (T2). However, the protocol types by item content, not by the scale's name. The unnamed source scale (Maral et al. [44]) could also be addiction-type. With no items to judge from, the protocol rule gives T4 (unclear).
codes.note: No item texts or development paper. The source might be Maral et al.'s Problematic ChatGPT Use Scale (possibly T1), but the reference list is missing, so this is unconfirmed. Recode after getting the R2863 items or the [44] reference.

codes.total_rationale: All 3 items are about relying on AI to carry out work tasks: handling work activities, making major work decisions, and checking and monitoring one's work. These are cases of handing task performance, decisions and cognition over to AI. No item covers addiction components such as salience, withdrawal or loss of control, and none covers emotional support or attachment.
quoted_items: I depended on AI to handle or help with work-related activities
I depended on AI to make major work-related decisions
I depended on AI to check and monitor my work
codes.note: Single total score with no subscales (R1277, R0901). All 3 declared items are printed. R0901 used a Korean back-translation. The development paper (Tang et al., 2023, HRM) was not checked. The label 'multiple-choice' in the instrument name was not checked against the items.

codes.total_rationale: The 22 items split about evenly. Functional (6) and cognitive (5) dependence items are about handing study work and thinking to AI, which is T2 (11 items). Loss-of-control items (6) and the emotional-dependence items (5) cover compulsive use, failed attempts to cut down, withdrawal-like distress and mood modification, which is T1-like (11 items). With no clear majority, the total score is T4. The higher-order factor is typed the same way.

subscales.name: Emotional dependence (5 items)
subscales.rationale: Despite the name, no companionship or attachment. Items describe mood modification ("feel calm and relaxed") and withdrawal-like distress when AI is unavailable for study ("anxious and frustrated", "uneasy or insecure"). One item ("feel supported") leans T3, so the majority is T1.

subscales.name: Functional dependence (6 items)
subscales.rationale: The items are about handing academic tasks to AI and being unable to manage without it ("I delegate almost all my academic tasks to AI", "can no longer manage complex academic tasks without the assistance of AI").

subscales.name: Cognitive dependence (5 items)
subscales.rationale: The items are about handing thinking and judgement to AI and losing independent analysis ("ask AI for answers directly without thinking for myself first", "letting AI make judgments and decisions for me").

subscales.name: Loss of control (6 items)
subscales.rationale: The items match addiction components: relapse or loss of control, compulsive use and withdrawal ("tried to reduce... never succeeded", "difficult to stop", "strong urge... irritable").

quoted_items: I have tried to reduce my use of AI, but I have never succeeded for long.
I delegate almost all my academic tasks to AI because it performs them faster and better than I do.
I often ask AI for answers directly without thinking for myself first.
I would feel anxious and frustrated if I couldn't use AI for my studies.
codes.note: The 'Emotional dependence' subscale was typed T1, not T3, because of what its items say: affect tied to using AI for study, with no relationship content. Three Wu 2026 items word things differently from the 22-item list. These could be paraphrases or translation variants.

codes.total_rationale: R0344 prints no item texts and reports no subscales. The only content is a one-line construct description: "feelings of closeness, dependence, and emotional investment in the AI companion". That points to emotional dependence (T3), but the protocol types by item content, so with no items the default is T4. This T4 is a default for missing information, not evidence that the items mix types.
codes.note: Likely T3 if items are found. The scale's name and description point to attachment to an AI companion. Xie & Pentina 2022 seems to be a qualitative Replika attachment study, so may have no items; please check. Recode to T3 if retrieved items confirm it.

codes.total_rationale: The five items don't share one type. Two are addiction-type: CAI3 (loss of control) and CAI4 (withdrawal-like anxiety). Two are about using the chatbot for tasks, which is functional or usage behaviour: CAI1 (intention to keep using it for academic tasks) and CAI2 (using it for academic issues). CAI5 (managing time) is unclear, at most a weak hint of conflict. With 2 addiction, 2 functional and 1 unclear, no type has a clear majority, so the total is T4.
quoted_items: Despite attempts, I find it challenging to reduce interactions with AI Chatbots.
I feel anxious when I am unable to use AI Chatbots for academic tasks.
I use AI Chatbots to address academic issues and enhance learning outcomes.
codes.note: No subscales; it was analysed as one construct. The cited source, Chen et al. (2020), is a review of AI in education, not a scale, so where the items came from is unclear. CAI4 is tied to academic tasks and could be read as T2.

codes.total_rationale: All 9 items are addiction criteria, one per DSM-5 IGD criterion: preoccupation, tolerance, withdrawal, persistence/failed control, escape/mood modification, problems, deception, displacement, conflict. No item asks about relying on AI to do tasks or think (T2) or about emotional support or attachment (T3). The withdrawal item is about distress at losing access, not about a relationship with the AI.
quoted_items: In the past year, have you… regularly felt dissatisfied because you wanted to spend more time using GenAI?
In the past year, have you… tried to reduce your use of GenAI, but failed?
In the past year, have you… regularly hidden your GenAI use from others?
codes.note: Only a unidimensional total score is reported. Each item covers one IGD criterion, but these are single items, not scored subscales, so no subscales are typed. The 9 items are the highest-loading ones from the 31-item version.

codes.total_rationale: R4677 prints no item texts and no subscales. It reports only a single total score called 'Problematic Use of Chatbot (GPIUS2)', adapted from Caplan (2010) and possibly shortened based on factor loadings. Because the type must come from item content, and there is no item text or subscale content to judge from, the protocol requires T4.
codes.note: For reviewer: original GPIUS2 covers preference for online social interaction, mood regulation, cognitive preoccupation, compulsive use and negative outcomes. Mostly addiction-type (likely T1 if kept intact), but kept items are unknown. Recode if the adapted items are obtained.

codes.total_rationale: Most of the 7 printed items are about emotional closeness and comfort, personal meaning, and turning to AI in place of people (no one to talk to, not being judged). That is attachment-like emotional reliance, so T3. Two normative-regard items are about treating AI respectfully. They are neither T1 nor T2 content, so the majority holds. 'Talk to AI when I face problems' could mean task help, but in context it reads as seeking support.
quoted_items: I feel a sense of closeness and comfort in my interactions with AI
When there's no one to talk to, I sometimes end up interacting with AI
I sometimes prefer talking to AI because I don't have to worry about being judged.
codes.note: Only 7 of 15 items printed. The three dimensions are not scored as subscales. The cited source (Sandeeshwara & Hartanto, 2025) is missing from the bibliography. The two normative-regard items (respect toward AI) are not dependence content. Total M=38.90, SD=11.46.

codes.total_rationale: This family covers two different instruments, so the total type differs by version. The 20-item CAIDS-20 total is mostly T1 (preoccupation, tolerance, loss of control, withdrawal, mood modification, negative consequences), with about 4 functional items (studies, decisions, thinking). The 12-item revision's total is split evenly: 6 functional (T2) and 6 emotional (T3) items, so it is T4. The pooled family spans T1, T2 and T3, so it is T4.

subscales.name: Uncontrollability (CAIDS-20)
subscales.rationale: Loss of control is an addiction component. Item content fits: 'cannot stop using', time exceeding plan, using more and more often. The item-to-dimension mapping is not printed, and the item count is reported as 6 in one place and 5 in another.

subscales.name: Withdrawal symptoms (CAIDS-20)
subscales.rationale: Withdrawal is an addiction component. Items: irritable, anxious, sense of loss, helpless when CAI is unavailable.

subscales.name: Mood modification (CAIDS-20)
subscales.rationale: Named after an addiction component, so T1 by rule. Its content (seeking comfort or relief when lonely or distressed) is close to emotional coping.

subscales.name: Negative impact (CAIDS-20)
subscales.rationale: Conflict and negative-consequences component: others complain, harm to studies or life, lost hobbies, fewer social contacts. Includes 1–2 items on reduced independent thinking (T2-like). Item count reported as 5 in one place and 6 in another.

subscales.name: Functional dependence (12-item revision)
subscales.rationale: Items cover relying on AI for academic tasks and decisions, turning to AI before thinking, difficulty without AI, and decline in independent thinking. One item (more time than planned) is T1-like. Item assignment is inferred from Appendix order.

subscales.name: Emotional dependence (12-item revision)
subscales.rationale: Items cover relieving negative emotions, companionship when lonely, feeling understood, confiding personal matters, and feeling empty when AI is unavailable. Item assignment is inferred from Appendix order.

quoted_items: I feel irritable when CAI is unavailable.
I feel like I cannot stop using CAI.
I am accustomed to depending on AI tools (e.g., DeepSeek) to complete academic tasks.
When feeling lonely, I turn to AI for companionship.
codes.note: Two different instruments are in this family. Code the CAIDS-20 total as T1 (majority) and the 12-item revision total as T4 (T2/T3 split evenly). The field orders do not line up across versions, so map reports to versions from the source reports.

codes.total_rationale: The report does not print any item text, and no subscales are reported. The protocol says type comes from item content, so the default is T4 (unclear). The scale name ('AI Addiction') and its citation to Pawlikowski et al. point toward T1. They cannot decide the type under the protocol's rule that item content decides type, not the name.
codes.note: Pawlikowski et al. probably wrote the 12-item short Internet Addiction Test (s-IAT, 2013), which matches the 12 declared items. If the AI_ADD items turn out to be s-IAT adaptations (loss of control, craving, social problems), recode as T1. Check the R2863 appendix or contact the authors.

codes.total_rationale: Item texts read in the paper (Table 8). At least 7 of 13 items are about relying on AI for academic tasks or instead of one's own critical thinking (exams, assignments, answering questions), so functional dependence is the clear majority. The minority items: one T3 ("support system and friend"), one about keeping access (close to T1 salience), two about trusting AI to be right, and one perceived-benefit item. None of these is large enough to change the type.
quoted_items: I rely on AI for my school assignments and tasks.
I depend more on AI than my critical thinking capacity
Because AI is usually faster, I often rely on it than my critical thinking
AI has been my support system and friend.
codes.note: No subscales; one total score is used, though the scree plot suggests about 4 factors. The paper says both 12 and 13 items, drops item 9, lists one item twice, and calls the scale 5-point but gives 4 anchors. Which version R0111 and R0770 used is unknown.

codes.total_rationale: All 12 printed items follow the DSM-5 Internet Gaming Disorder criteria: preoccupation, withdrawal, tolerance, failed attempts to cut down, loss of interest, use despite problems, deception, escape and negative consequences (sleep loss, procrastination). No item is about using AI for tasks or about an emotional bond. The 'alleviate helplessness or anxiety' item is the escape/mood-modification criterion, so it counts as T1.

subscales.name: Salience
subscales.rationale: Named after an addiction component (salience/preoccupation). Typed from the subscale name only, because items per dimension were not reported.

subscales.name: Conflict
subscales.rationale: Named after an addiction component (conflict). Typed from the subscale name only; item assignment not reported.

subscales.name: Withdrawal
subscales.rationale: Named after an addiction component (withdrawal). Typed from the subscale name only; item assignment not reported.

subscales.name: Problematic consequences
subscales.rationale: Covers the negative-consequences component of addiction. Typed from the subscale name only; item assignment not reported.

quoted_items: I experience anxiety or irritability when unable to access ChatGPT
I have attempted to reduce my ChatGPT usage, but without success
I constantly have thoughts related to ChatGPT lingering in my mind
I suffer from sleep deprivation due to excessive use of ChatGPT
codes.note: The four dimensions were named in only one report; the others scored a single, one-factor total. The Turkish version keeps 9 of the 11 items. One report changes 'ChatGPT' to 'AI chatbot'. None of these changes alter the T1 typing.

codes.total_rationale: The only item printed in R1122 is about unsuccessful attempts to cut down, which is the relapse / loss-of-control component of behavioural addiction. The report says the scale applies a symptom-based framework from behavioural addiction research (salience, tolerance, mood modification, withdrawal, conflict, unsuccessful attempts to reduce use). This framework description matches Griffiths-type components. Nothing in the report points to functional or emotional dependence content.
quoted_items: I tried to cut down on my use of AI without success
codes.note: Only one verbatim item is available, so the call also relies on the report's framework description. The full item set and the Zhang et al. development paper were not available. The report names no subscales. Confirm T1 against the full item list if it can be obtained.

codes.total_rationale: All 8 items are printed in the reports. They split about evenly between addiction-type and functional content. Addiction-type: withdrawal (item 1), tolerance (item 7), compulsive or salient use (item 6, arguably items 2 and 5). Functional: trouble getting information without the AI (item 3), over-reliance even on easy tasks (item 4), life troublesome without it (item 8). Neither type has a clear majority, so the total is mixed (T4).
quoted_items: I feel restless or uncomfortable if I cannot use AI chatbots
AICDS7—Cada vez dedico más tiempo al uso de chatbots con IA.
AICDS4—Incluso cuando me enfrento a tareas o trabajos que podría completar fácilmente por mi cuenta, tiendo a buscar ayuda en los chatbots con IA.
Yapay zekâ sohbet botlarını kullanamadığımda, gerekli bilgilere ulaşmakta zorlanırım.
codes.note: One factor, no subscales. One report says it rests on Griffiths' components, but the item content is about half addiction-type and half functional reliance. Item 5 (preferring AI to people) could also be read as companionship (T3). The development paper was not available.

codes.total_rationale: The five items were adapted from core smartphone-addiction symptoms (Revised Smartphone Addiction Scale). Item-level results describe them as subjective dependence, excessive use, harm to studies or relationships (conflict), withdrawal, and loss of control. At least four are behavioural-addiction components; the generic 'subjective dependence' item does not change the majority. No item is about delegating tasks or emotional companionship.
quoted_items: I have tried to reduce the amount of time I spend on AI but failed
I feel anxious and upset when I cannot use artificial intelligence.
I feel anxious when I am unable to use artificial intelligence
codes.note: Unidimensional, no subscales. Only 2 distinct items printed verbatim (third quote is a variant wording). The other 3 are known from item-level prevalence results; full items are in Appendix Table S2, not retrieved.

codes.total_rationale: No item texts are printed in the included report and no development paper is available. There are no subscales, so there is no subscale content to judge from. The construct label "AI dependency" alone does not decide the type, because the protocol types by item content. With no item text and no subscale content, the rule assigns T4 (unclear).
codes.note: The 3-item construct was self-authored (Pradeep, 2026) and sits next to academic self-efficacy, confidence and anxiety constructs. That context hints at functional (T2) academic reliance, but this is not confirmed. Get the item texts from the authors or supplementary files to retype it.

codes.total_rationale: T1, addiction-type. Adapted from the Smartphone Addiction Scale – Short Version. Reported content: loss of control, withdrawal, reduced efficiency (a negative consequence). Two of three printed items are clearly T1: withdrawal ("anxious and upset when I cannot use") and loss of control ("tried to reduce... but failed"). "I rely too much on AI" reads like T2 over-reliance but is a minority item, so the majority type is T1. Only 3 of 8 items are printed.
quoted_items: I feel anxious and upset when I cannot use artificial intelligence
I have tried to reduce the amount of time I spend on AI but failed
I rely too much on AI
codes.note: Only 3 of 8 items are printed. No subscales were reported, so only the total score is typed. 'I rely too much on AI' is a T2-type over-reliance item. The rest of the evidence (the SAS-SV source and the listed components) points to T1. No development paper was available.

codes.total_rationale: Low confidence, based on partial items. The single score is described as excessive use of ChatGPT for academic purposes. The one clearly typeable item is functional: preferring ChatGPT for finding information. 'I would feel uncomfortable without ChatGPT' could mean trouble working without it (T2) or withdrawal (T1). Only 2 of the 5–6 items are known, and the I-PACE addiction framing raises the chance of T1 content, so T4 is a reasonable alternative.
quoted_items: I always prefer to use ChatGPT to find information
Me sentiría incómodo sin ChatGPT
codes.note: Only 2 items known; reports disagree on count (5 vs 6). Development paper (Ye et al., 2024, EAIT) needed to confirm: check the remaining items for withdrawal/conflict/loss-of-control content (would shift to T1 or T4). Single score, no subscales.

codes.total_rationale: I read all 7 items. Six are about relying on generative AI for work tasks: completing tasks, having trouble working without it, turning to it first for problems, getting ideas from it, using its output with little change, and letting it take over tasks the person used to do. That is functional or cognitive dependence. Only one item ('feel uncomfortable when I cannot access') sounds like withdrawal (T1). The majority type is T2.
quoted_items: I find it difficult to complete my work tasks without generative AI.
When I face a work problem, I turn to generative AI first.
I now use generative AI for tasks I previously did on my own.
codes.note: Single-factor scale; items are averaged. One item of 7 ('I feel uncomfortable when I cannot access generative AI at work') is like withdrawal (T1), but it is outnumbered. This is a work-context adaptation of Morales-García et al. (2024). The development paper was not available.

codes.total_rationale: No item texts are available. All nine reported dimensions map directly onto the DSM-5 Internet Gaming Disorder criteria (preoccupation, tolerance, withdrawal, persistence, escape, problems, deception, displacement, conflict), and the instrument is framed as measuring problematic use. Since every subscale is addiction-type, the total score is T1. This typing rests on the subscale names only, not on item content.

subscales.name: Preoccupation
subscales.rationale: DSM-5 IGD criterion; salience/preoccupation component. Typed from the subscale name only.

subscales.name: Tolerance
subscales.rationale: DSM-5 IGD criterion; tolerance component. Typed from the subscale name only.

subscales.name: Withdrawal
subscales.rationale: DSM-5 IGD criterion; withdrawal component. Typed from the subscale name only.

subscales.name: Persistence
subscales.rationale: DSM-5 IGD criterion (loss of control / continued excessive use despite problems). Typed from the subscale name only.

subscales.name: Escape
subscales.rationale: DSM-5 IGD criterion; mood modification (using to escape negative mood). Typed from the subscale name only.

subscales.name: Problems
subscales.rationale: DSM-5 IGD criterion; continued use despite psychosocial problems (negative consequences). Typed from the subscale name only.

subscales.name: Deception
subscales.rationale: DSM-5 IGD criterion; deceiving others about the amount of use. Typed from the subscale name only.

subscales.name: Displacement
subscales.rationale: DSM-5 IGD criterion; loss of interest in other activities. Typed from the subscale name only.

subscales.name: Conflict
subscales.rationale: DSM-5 IGD criterion; jeopardised relationships or opportunities (conflict). Typed from the subscale name only.

codes.note: R4232 prints no item texts; the development paper is unavailable; item counts per dimension are not given. The 31 items came from a 40-item pool built partly from interviews, so a few may be functional or emotional. Check this if the item texts become available.

codes.total_rationale: I typed this as T2 (functional dependence) because every item in the development paper's item table is about using, relying on or trusting AI to do academic or cognitive tasks: reading, writing and maths or problem solving. No item covers addiction components such as salience, withdrawal, loss of control or conflict. No item covers emotional support or attachment. Many items describe how often AI is used for a task rather than difficulty working without it, but they are still about tasks.

subscales.name: Writing (11 items)
subscales.rationale: The items are about relying on AI for spelling and grammar, generating ideas, paraphrasing, proofreading and summarising. This is handing writing tasks over to AI.

subscales.name: Reading (10 items)
subscales.rationale: The items are about using AI summaries, comprehension tools and information extraction to understand texts. This is relying on AI for reading tasks.

subscales.name: Numeracy/Arithmetic (12 items)
subscales.rationale: The items are about relying on or trusting AI to solve maths problems, check calculations and support numeracy decisions. This is handing problem solving over to AI.

quoted_items: I rely on AI algorithms to solve complex mathematical problems beyond basic arithmetic.
I depend on AI-powered paraphrasing tools to rephrase sentences in my written work.
I use AI-generated summaries to understand lengthy articles or documents.
I trust AI-generated solutions for problem-solving.
codes.note: Item codes don't match: WAI15 is kept and WAI16 removed, but neither is in the item table. The type is unaffected because every candidate item is task-based. Many items measure how often AI is used rather than true dependence.

codes.total_rationale: The total is the sum of items 1–5 and 7–11 (item 6 is left out), and those 10 items split three ways. Four are emotional (1, 2, 3, 7): confiding in AI and preferring it to people. Three are functional (4, 5, 8): uncritical acceptance, anxiety at doing tasks without AI, avoiding tasks without AI. Three are addiction-type (9 withdrawal, 10 loss of control over time, 11 hiding use). Item 3 could also count as mood modification. No type has a clear majority, so T4.

subscales.name: F1 Соціально-емоційна залежність (items 1,2,3,7)
subscales.rationale: Items 1, 2 and 7 are about confiding in the AI, preferring it to people, and telling it secrets, which is emotional dependence. Item 3 (turning to AI to calm down under stress) is emotional support, with some mood-modification flavour. Majority T3.

subscales.name: F2 Поведінково-когнітивна залежність (items 4,5,8,9,10,11)
subscales.rationale: Items 4, 5 and 8 are functional over-reliance (T2). Items 9 (discomfort without access, i.e. withdrawal), 10 (more time than planned) and 11 (hiding how much they use it) are addiction components (T1). The split is 3:3, so neither type is a majority.

subscales.name: ІКМ Critical Thinking Indicator (item 6, reverse-scored, outside total)
subscales.rationale: This is one reverse-scored item about checking AI information against other sources. A low score means relying on AI output without checking it, which is cognitive over-reliance.

codes.note: The scale is called an 'Addiction Scale', but the items are mostly not addiction-type. Item 3 sits between T3 (emotional support) and T1 (mood modification); either reading leaves the total T4. Typing is based on all 11 printed items; the development paper was not available.

codes.total_rationale: Single 5-item construct; reports print two item versions. Spanish AID1–AID5 is mostly T2 (difficulty without AI, growing reliance, using AI when unnecessary, expected performance loss), with one withdrawal-like item. English version: 3 addiction-type items (worry about not using AI, trouble controlling time, needing AI more and more) vs 2 T2 reliance items. Types are split across the family, no clear majority, so T4.
quoted_items: Me resulta difícil realizar tareas académicas sin usar inteligencia artificial
Do you find it difficult to control the amount of time you spend using AI?
Do you feel the need to use AI more and more frequently to maintain your academic performance?
Me siento incómodo(a) cuando no tengo acceso a herramientas de inteligencia artificial para estudiar
codes.note: Alone, the Spanish version would be T2 (4 T2, 1 withdrawal-like); the English version leans T1 (3 of 5). Original version unknown (no development paper). In the 27-item ASAIDAS only the 5-item AID score was typed. GAID5 seems dropped in one report.

codes.total_rationale: The second-order total combines three different kinds of content. Behavioural Dyscontrol (10/21 items, about 48%) is addiction-type: neglected tasks and loss of control. Cognitive Impairment (5 items) is functional, about weakened problem solving. Emotional Attachment (6 items) is attachment or mood modification. No type is a clear majority of the 21 items. The pool was built on Griffiths' model, but the scale also covers cognitive and emotional content. So the total is mixed (T4).

subscales.name: Davranışsal Kontrolsüzlük / Behavioural Dyscontrol (10 items)
subscales.rationale: The printed item is about neglecting daily tasks because of AI use, which is Griffiths' conflict / negative-consequences component. The subscale name also refers to loss of control.

subscales.name: Duygusal Bağlanma / Emotional Attachment (6 items)
subscales.rationale: The name points to T3, but the one printed item ('makes me feel powerful') reads as mood modification (T1), not support or companionship. We have 1 of 6 items, so the content is unclear.

subscales.name: Bilişsel Zayıflama / Cognitive Impairment (5 items)
subscales.rationale: The printed item says AI use has weakened the person's own real-life problem-solving skills. That is about delegating thinking and depending on AI to think (functional dependence).

Yapay zekâ uygulamalarını kullanmak beni güçlü hissettirir

codes.note: Only 3 of 21 items are printed. I matched each to a subscale by content; the report doesn't assign them. Item count is inconsistent (21 declared vs 25 in abstract), and the development paper isn't available. Emotional Attachment may be T1 (mood modification), not T3.

codes.total_rationale: Most of the 12 items are about relying on GenAI for tasks and thinking. Seven are clearly functional: lacking confidence without AI, using AI first even for doable tasks, not seeking alternatives, AI as the main choice, AI first on complex problems, no need to memorise, worry about solving alone. Three trust or efficiency items lean functional. Two are T1 (withdrawal-like anxiety, tolerance-like increasing time). None are emotional or companionship items.

subscales.name: Affective Dependency
subscales.rationale: The report does not say which items belong to this subscale. The likely items are anxiety when unable to use AI (T1-type withdrawal) and trust in the AI's privacy and outputs (attitudes). None are about emotional bonds or companionship, so it is not T3. The type is unclear.

subscales.name: Behavioural Dependency
subscales.rationale: Tentative, because the item mapping is not reported. The likely items are using AI first even for doable tasks, AI as the main choice for study or work, AI as the first thought on complex problems (T2), and increasing time spent (T1-type tolerance). That gives a T2 majority.

subscales.name: Cognitive Dependency
subscales.rationale: The mapping is not reported, but the likely items are about delegating thinking: lacking confidence in one's own answers, not memorising, worrying about solving problems alone, and not seeking alternatives. These describe delegating cognition.

quoted_items: Even for tasks I am capable of completing independently, I give priority to using Generative AI to solve them.
Without the assistance of Generative AI, I lack confidence in the answers I arrive at through my own thinking.
I worry that my ability to solve problems independently would be insufficient without Generative AI.
I feel noticeably anxious or unsettled when I am unable to use Generative AI.
codes.note: The item-to-subscale mapping is not reported, so subscale types are inferred and tentative. Two items are T1-type (anxious when unable to use; time increasing). Two trust items fit no type well. The development paper was not available.
